verdict.reasoning: Patient reports 3 days of diarrhea (“It was three days ago”) with vomiting (“I've been throwing up”) and feeling feverish (“I've been running a serious temperature. I'm literally boiling.”).

She states the diarrhea started watery then became very loose (“it's very loose but it started as being very watery”) and that today she has been to the toilet at least four times (“Today alone, I've been at least four time.”).

She feels feverish (“I've been running a serious temperature. I'm literally boiling.”) and says she is vomiting everything including liquids (“Not even water, not even my tea, not even any liquid stuff. I've just been throwing up everything.”).

Pain is periumbilical (“towards my navel area… almost like the center of my navel”) and intermittent with urge to defecate (“it does come. When it comes, I feel this strong urge to go to the loo, and then… it comes”). Description is consistent with intermittent crampy pain and urge to defecate.
When asked about blood in stool or urine, patient says “No blood.”
She reports last vomiting was after breakfast about two hours ago (“I was sick just after trying… to have breakfast this morning, so maybe about two hours ago.”).
She last passed urine about an hour ago (“an hour ago”) and states she did not look at the color (“To be honest, I have a look so I really couldn't say.”).
She says her brother has similar symptoms and mentions a school outbreak (“my brother… has actually been having similar symptoms… and he does say like everyone in school's got this”).
She denies travel (“No, but then, um, my, um my brother…”) and reports a normal diet (“Yeah, I eat well, normally.”).

She used ORS three times a day for two days (“I've taken that, like, um, three times a day for the past two days”) and states symptoms are not improving because she vomits everything (“they're not getting any better… I've been vomiting literally everything I take, so… I doubt that even that had the chance to work”).

She reports no prior abdominal problems except menstrual cramps (“apart from the fact that this one is giving me abdominal pains, no previous abdominal pains before. Obviously I get the odd… menstrual cramps”).
She takes vitamin D daily and ibuprofen for menstrual cramps as needed (“I take… vitamin D, every day… for my menstrual cramps… I might take… an ibuprofen just to ease the pain”).

She is a graphics designer (“A graphics designer”), is working from home because of illness (“I'm working from home today because I can't… be out for work”), and lives with her brother and mum (“I live with my brother and my mum.”).
She does not smoke and drinks alcohol occasionally (“I don't smoke, but, you know, I have a pint from time to time.”).
When asked about rash, she denies it (“No, no rash, no, nothing that, um.”).

Doctor states it sounds like infectious gastroenteritis, viral or foodborne (“it sounds like it might be some, an infectious gastroenteritis… usually caused by a virus. But, it can be from something you've eaten, as well.”), and the symptoms listed (3 days of diarrhea, vomiting, fever, crampy abdominal pain) match the history described.

Doctor notes risk of dehydration from not keeping fluids down but that urine output is present (“if you're not keeping fluid down, then you can get dehydrated… it's a positive sign that you passed urine an hour ago. So, you're obviously still… hydrated enough to pass urine.”).

Doctor advises continuing ORS in tiny frequent sips (“keep going with the rehydration salts. Just tiny sips constantly… just tiny, tiny sips but just keep going with it.”) and simple oral intake as tolerated is implied.

Doctor recommends simple foods like toast or biscuits and to avoid fruit, vegetables, and milk (“have anything, like toast or biscuit… Avoid, um, fruit, vegetables, uh, milk”), but BRAT diet terminology is not used and bananas/rice are not mentioned. Stating “BRAT” specifically adds content not in transcript.

Doctor plans to obtain stool sample for testing (“important to get a sample of the stool, so we can make sure that you haven't got a nasty bacterial infection which needs specific treatment”) consistent with culture/PCR per protocol.

Doctor states she should be seen urgently in clinic to assess hydration and send the stool sample (“we should see you so that we can check your hydration and, um, get that sample sent off as soon as possible… we can make you an urgent appointment”).

Doctor only specifies going to A&E if feeling more unwell (“if, in the meantime, you're feeling more unwell, then we would get you seen urgently in A and E”). Detailed criteria such as reduced urine output, persistent high fever, blood in stool, confusion, or symptoms >7 days are not mentioned.

Working from home and rest are described by the patient as current behavior, but the doctor does not explicitly advise “continue working from home and rest as needed.” This is a new management recommendation not stated.

Doctor says follow-up should be booked via support line and to call back if more unwell (“you'll have to book an appointment through the support line” and “you can call us back in the meantime” / “if… you're feeling more unwell, then we would get you seen urgently in A and E”).
